subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: New cells only come from cells dividing
Cytokinesis is usually equal, but not always
DNA is replicated once before either division
Chromosomes condense and are moved by microtubules in both divisions
Reading the phase from a diagram or micrograph
Meiosis makes variation: random orientation and crossing over
The cell cycle: G1, S, G2, mitosis, cytokinesis
Interphase is busy, not resting
Mutations in cell-cycle genes drive uncontrolled division
Proteins bind promoters and enhancers to control transcription
Cells differentiate by expressing different genes, not by changing DNA
Expression patterns can be inherited if tags stay in place
Most tags are wiped from gametes, but not all: ligers and tigons
Identical twins reveal environmental effects on expression
How water dissolves ions and polar molecules
Finding a tissue's isotonic concentration, and judging the data
Cells with walls become turgid or plasmolyse
Isotonic solutions in medicine
Water moves from higher to lower water potential
Explaining turgor and plasmolysis with potentials

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes how new cells are generated in a living organism?
options: A parent cell divides to produce two daughter cells, and everything the parent contained is shared out between them.
A parent cell produces two daughter cells and then goes on living alongside them as a third cell.
A parent cell splits at one moment into many small daughter cells, which then grow to full size in the tissue.
A parent cell splits its cytoplasm into two halves, each of which then assembles a nucleus of its own from the cytoplasm.
optionWhy: In all living organisms new cells arise by division of a parent (mother) cell into two daughter cells. The parent cell does not persist; its whole contents are divided between the two daughters.
A student who reads 'mother' and 'daughter' as a human family picks this. The parent cell is the material from which the two daughter cells are made; no third cell remains.
A student who pictures one cell fragmenting into many picks this. Each division produces exactly two daughter cells; large numbers come from repeated divisions.
A student who thinks a nucleus can be built from scratch picks this. The nucleus divides first by mitosis or meiosis, and each daughter cell receives one of the two nuclei produced.
questions.explain: In all living organisms new cells arise by division of a parent (mother) cell into two daughter cells. The parent cell does not persist; its whole contents are divided between the two daughters.

questions.q: Which statement about the division of the cytoplasm between two daughter cells is correct?
options: The cytoplasm is divided equally in every cell division, so that each daughter cell receives exactly half of each type of organelle.
A daughter cell that receives no mitochondria can synthesize new ones from proteins made on its ribosomes, so none need be shared.
When cytoplasm is divided unequally, the daughter cell that receives more cytoplasm also receives the larger share of the chromosomes.
Each daughter cell must receive at least one mitochondrion, because mitochondria form only by division of existing ones.
optionWhy: A student who has only seen symmetrical diagrams picks this. Division of the cytoplasm is usually equal but not in all cases; oogenesis and yeast budding are unequal.
A student who thinks a cell can build any structure from raw materials picks this. Mitochondria arise only from existing mitochondria, which is exactly why each daughter must receive at least one.
A student who equates the size of a cell with its share of everything picks this. The chromosomes are shared equally by nuclear division; only the cytoplasm is divided unequally.
Mitochondria, like chloroplasts, can only be made by division of a pre-existing organelle. A daughter cell that received none could not make any, so at least one must be passed to each cell.
questions.explain: Mitochondria, like chloroplasts, can only be made by division of a pre-existing organelle. A daughter cell that received none could not make any, so at least one must be passed to each cell.

questions.q: What is the structure of a chromosome after DNA replication and before anaphase?
options: Two DNA molecules, one inherited from each parent, joined together to form a homologous pair.
A single elongated DNA molecule, which is not copied to form a second chromatid until prophase.
Two separate chromosomes, each with one DNA molecule, so that the chromosome number has doubled.
Two identical elongated DNA molecules, the sister chromatids, held together at the centromere.
optionWhy: A student who reads the X-shaped diagram as a homologous pair picks this. The two chromatids are identical copies made by replication; homologous chromosomes are separate chromosomes.
A student who thinks the second chromatid appears when chromosomes condense picks this. Replication is complete in interphase; prophase only makes the two existing chromatids visible.
A student who counts each chromatid as a chromosome picks this. Until anaphase the two chromatids are held together and count as one chromosome, so the chromosome number is unchanged.
After replication each chromosome consists of two elongated DNA molecules (chromatids), exact copies of each other, which remain held together until anaphase.
questions.explain: After replication each chromosome consists of two elongated DNA molecules (chromatids), exact copies of each other, which remain held together until anaphase.

questions.q: How is the DNA of a eukaryotic chromosome condensed before nuclear division?
options: The double helix itself twists ever more tightly, with no proteins involved, until the molecule is short enough to be seen.
The DNA is wound around histone proteins, and the fibre so formed is supercoiled into a much shorter, thicker structure.
The DNA is already packed as a condensed chromosome throughout the cycle; staining at division merely makes it visible.
The DNA is copied, and the two new copies pack tightly against each other to form the short, visible chromosome.
optionWhy: A student who hears 'supercoiling' as more of the helix's own coiling picks this. The naked helix cannot be packed into a chromosome; the coiling is of DNA wound around histone proteins.
Condensation depends on histones: DNA wound around histones forms nucleosomes, and the DNA–protein fibre is then coiled and supercoiled, shortening the chromosome so it can be moved without tangling.
A student who takes the karyotype image as the permanent state of DNA picks this. Between divisions the DNA is extended for transcription and replication; it condenses only for nuclear division.
A student who confuses replication with condensation picks this. Replication happens in interphase and produces two chromatids; it is supercoiling around histones, not copying, that shortens them.
questions.explain: Condensation depends on histones: DNA wound around histones forms nucleosomes, and the DNA–protein fibre is then coiled and supercoiled, shortening the chromosome so it can be moved without tangling.

questions.q: Two cells are seen in a stained micrograph of a root tip. Cell 1 has an intact nucleus in which no separate chromosomes can be distinguished. Cell 2 has no nuclear envelope, and its condensed chromosomes lie in a single line across the middle of the cell. Which identification is correct?
options: Cell 1 is in prophase; cell 2 is in metaphase.
Cell 1 is in interphase; cell 2 is in metaphase.
Cell 1 is in interphase; cell 2 is in prophase.
Cell 1 is in interphase; cell 2 is in early anaphase.
optionWhy: A student who counts interphase as the first stage of mitosis picks this. Prophase is recognized by condensed, visible chromosomes; a cell with an intact nucleus and no distinct chromosomes is in interphase.

An intact nucleus with no distinct chromosomes shows a cell between divisions, in interphase. Condensed chromosomes aligned on one plane at the equator, with the nuclear envelope gone, define metaphase.

A student who identifies prophase by 'condensed but not yet separating' picks this. Chromosomes aligned in a single plane at the equator are the defining feature of metaphase; in prophase they are scattered.

A student who has swapped the names of the two middle phases picks this. Anaphase begins when the chromatids separate and move apart; while the chromosomes are still aligned on the equator the cell is in metaphase.
questions.explain: An intact nucleus with no distinct chromosomes shows a cell between divisions, in interphase. Condensed chromosomes aligned on one plane at the equator, with the nuclear envelope gone, define metaphase.

questions.q: Which statement about crossing over is correct?
options: Sister chromatids of one chromosome exchange lengths of DNA, so that the two chromatids come to differ from each other.
The exchange of DNA alters the base sequence at the exchanged region, creating new alleles of the genes found there.
The exchange between chromatids decides which chromosome of each pair moves to each pole of the cell in anaphase I.
Non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes exchange lengths of DNA, producing new combinations of alleles.
optionWhy: A student who remembers 'chromatids exchange segments' without 'non-sister' picks this. Sister chromatids are identical, so exchanging DNA between them could produce no new combination.
A student who confuses new combinations with new alleles picks this. Crossing over exchanges existing alleles between homologues; new alleles arise only by mutation.
A student who merges crossing over with random orientation picks this. Which homologue goes to which pole is decided by the random orientation of the bivalent at metaphase I, a separate process.

Crossing over occurs in prophase I, while homologous chromosomes are paired as a bivalent. Non-sister chromatids exchange corresponding lengths of DNA, so each chromatid carries a new combination of the alleles present on the two homologues.
questions.explain: Crossing over occurs in prophase I, while homologous chromosomes are paired as a bivalent. Non-sister chromatids exchange corresponding lengths of DNA, so each chromatid carries a new combination of the alleles present on the two homologues.

questions.q: Which statement correctly gives the sequence of phases in the cell cycle?
options: Interphase, made up of G1 and G2, is followed by S, in which the DNA is replicated, and then by mitosis and cytokinesis.
Interphase, a resting period in which the cell is inactive, is followed by mitosis and then by cytokinesis.
Interphase, made up of G1, S and G2 in that order, is followed by mitosis and then by cytokinesis.
Mitosis, which occupies most of the cycle, is followed by cytokinesis and then by a short interphase of G1, S and G2.
optionWhy: A student who places replication just before mitosis picks this. S phase lies between G1 and G2; by G2 the DNA has already been replicated and the cell is growing and preparing for mitosis.
A student who takes 'interphase' to mean a pause picks this. Interphase is metabolically active: the cell grows, synthesizes proteins and DNA and increases its organelles.
The cell cycle by which cells proliferate runs G1, S and G2 (the stages of interphase), then mitosis, then cytokinesis; the daughter cells then enter G1 of the next cycle.
A student who judges the length of a phase by how much is taught about it picks this. Interphase takes most of the cycle; mitosis is a short part of it, and the sequence is interphase first.
questions.explain: The cell cycle by which cells proliferate runs G1, S and G2 (the stages of interphase), then mitosis, then cytokinesis; the daughter cells then enter G1 of the next cycle.

questions.q: The mass of DNA per nucleus was measured for many cells from a growing tissue. Most nuclei contained 6.0 pg, a smaller group contained 12.0 pg, and a few contained values between 6.0 and 12.0 pg. Which interpretation is correct?
options: The 12.0 pg nuclei have twice as many chromosomes as the 6.0 pg nuclei, so they belong to cells that have just completed mitosis.
The intermediate values are measurement errors, because the DNA content of a nucleus does not change during the inactivity of interphase.
The 12.0 pg nuclei are in prophase, when the DNA is replicated to form the chromatids, and every interphase nucleus contains 6.0 pg.
The 6.0 pg nuclei are in G1, the 12.0 pg nuclei have completed S phase and are in G2 or entering mitosis, and the intermediate values are nuclei in S phase.
optionWhy: A student who equates DNA mass with chromosome number picks this. Replication doubles the DNA without changing the chromosome number, and cells that have just completed mitosis are back at 6.0 pg.

A student who thinks interphase is a resting phase picks this. Interphase includes S phase, in which DNA is actively synthesized, so intermediate values are expected in cells caught during replication.
A student who thinks chromatids are made in prophase picks this. Replication is completed in S phase of interphase, so G2 nuclei already contain 12.0 pg before mitosis begins.

DNA is synthesized during S phase of interphase, so a nucleus that has completed replication contains twice the DNA of a G1 nucleus, and a nucleus caught during replication contains an intermediate amount. The chromosome number is the same in all of them.
questions.explain: DNA is synthesized during S phase of interphase, so a nucleus that has completed replication contains twice the DNA of a G1 nucleus, and a nucleus caught during replication contains an intermediate amount. The chromosome number is the same in all of them.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes how mutations in genes that control the cell cycle lead to uncontrolled cell division?
options: Mutations make both proto-oncogenes and tumour suppressor genes over-active, so both kinds of gene then stimulate division more strongly.
An oncogene is a gene that a healthy cell does not possess, so uncontrolled division can begin only when one is introduced from outside.
A mutation can turn a proto-oncogene into an oncogene that drives division, or stop a tumour suppressor gene restraining division.
Mutations in cell-cycle genes occur in gametes, so uncontrolled division appears only in the offspring that inherit the mutated gene.
optionWhy: A student who treats all cancer-related mutations alike picks this. A tumour suppressor mutation is a loss of function: the product that would halt division no longer works.
A student who reads 'oncogene' as a foreign cancer gene picks this. Every cell has proto-oncogenes; a mutation in one of the cell's own genes converts it into an oncogene.

Proto-oncogenes are normal genes whose products promote the cell cycle; a mutation can make one an oncogene with an over-active product. Tumour suppressor genes restrain the cycle; mutations that disable them remove that restraint. Either change results in uncontrolled division.
A student who assumes all mutations are inherited picks this. Most such mutations arise in somatic cells and cause a tumour in the individual in which they occur; they are not passed on.
questions.explain: Proto-oncogenes are normal genes whose products promote the cell cycle; a mutation can make one an oncogene with an over-active product. Tumour suppressor genes restrain the cycle; mutations that disable them remove that restraint. Either change results in uncontrolled division.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the promoter of a gene in a eukaryotic cell?
options: The first part of the gene to be transcribed, which codes for the first amino acids of the polypeptide
A protein that binds to an enhancer sequence and increases the rate of transcription of the gene
A sequence near the start of the gene to which transcription factors and RNA polymerase bind
A base sequence that RNA polymerase binds to by itself, with no other proteins required
optionWhy: A student who pictures the gene as one continuous piece of code picks this. The promoter lies upstream of the transcribed region and is not copied into mRNA, so it codes for nothing.
A student who thinks promoters are proteins picks this. The promoter is a DNA sequence; the proteins that bind to enhancers and promoters are transcription factors.
The promoter is a specific base sequence in DNA. Transcription factors bind to it first, and this allows RNA polymerase to bind and begin transcription of the gene downstream.
A student who learned transcription as 'RNA polymerase binds and copies' picks this. In eukaryotic cells transcription factors must bind to the promoter before RNA polymerase can attach.
questions.explain: The promoter is a specific base sequence in DNA. Transcription factors bind to it first, and this allows RNA polymerase to bind and begin transcription of the gene downstream.

questions.q: Which statement about epigenesis, the development of patterns of differentiation in a multicellular organism, is correct?
options: Cells become different from each other because each type keeps only the genes it needs
Cells become different from each other through changes in gene expression, not in DNA sequence
Cells become different from each other through mutations that alter the sequences of their genes
Cells become different from each other by expressing all of their genes at different rates
optionWhy: A student who thinks differentiated cells discard unused genes picks this. Every body cell retains the complete genome; differentiation changes which genes are expressed, not which are present.

All the cells derive from one zygote and share a genome. Patterns of differentiation develop as different genes are switched on and off in different cells; the base sequences are not altered, so phenotype but not genotype changes.
A student who treats any developmental change in DNA activity as a mutation picks this. Epigenetic changes leave the base sequence unaltered, so genotype is unchanged while phenotype changes.
A student who assumes every gene is in use in every cell picks this. No cell expresses all of its genes; many genes are not transcribed at all in a given cell type.
questions.explain: All the cells derive from one zygote and share a genome. Patterns of differentiation develop as different genes are switched on and off in different cells; the base sequences are not altered, so phenotype but not genotype changes.

questions.q: In a skin cell, the promoter of gene G is methylated and the gene is not expressed. The cell divides by mitosis. What is the most likely state of gene G in the daughter cells, and why?
options: Expressed, because epigenetic tags are lost whenever DNA is replicated
Not expressed, because the methylation has changed the base sequence of the gene
Not expressed, because the methyl tags remained in place through mitosis
Not expressed in the person's children, because the tags pass to offspring
optionWhy: A student who thinks only the base sequence survives cell division picks this. Methylation patterns can be maintained through mitosis, which is how differentiated cells produce daughter cells of the same type.
A student who treats methylation as a mutation picks this. The daughter cells do inherit the silenced state, but the base sequence of gene G is not altered; only the tag is passed on.

Epigenetic tags such as promoter methylation can remain in place during mitosis, so the daughter cells inherit the same pattern of gene expression. The base sequence of gene G is unchanged; this is epigenetic inheritance.

A student who thinks acquired epigenetic changes go to the next generation picks this. A tag in a skin cell is passed only to that cell's daughter cells; reaching offspring would require the tag to be in a gamete.
questions.explain: Epigenetic tags such as promoter methylation can remain in place during mitosis, so the daughter cells inherit the same pattern of gene expression. The base sequence of gene G is unchanged; this is epigenetic inheritance.

questions.q: Why is it important that most epigenetic tags are removed from the DNA of the sperm and the ovum?
options: So that no epigenetic tag from either parent is able to affect the offspring's cells
So that the cells of the embryo can develop a fresh pattern of differentiation
So that the base sequence of the offspring's DNA is restored to normal
So that every gene in the zygote is switched off until it is needed
optionWhy: A student who thinks the gametes are wiped completely clean picks this. Most but not all tags are removed; some remain, and these affect how certain genes are expressed according to the parent that supplied them.

Removing most of the tags from the gametes means the embryo is not committed to the expression patterns of the parents' cells, so its cells can differentiate into every cell type. The tags that are not removed are the exception that makes ligers and tigons differ.

A student who thinks tags alter the sequence picks this. Epigenetic tags do not change the base sequence, so there is nothing in the sequence to restore; removing tags changes only the pattern of expression.

A student who takes tags to be 'on' labels picks this. Many tags, such as promoter methylation, repress genes, so removing them does not switch every gene off; it resets the pattern so that a new one can be established.
questions.explain: Removing most of the tags from the gametes means the embryo is not committed to the expression patterns of the parents' cells, so its cells can differentiate into every cell type. The tags that are not removed are the exception that makes ligers and tigons differ.

questions.q: In a study, the DNA methylation patterns of pairs of monozygotic twins were compared. Three-year-old twins had almost identical patterns. Fifty-year-old twins showed large differences, and the differences were greatest in pairs who had spent the most years living apart. What is the best interpretation?
options: The methylation differences show that the older twins' DNA base sequences had changed
The older pairs cannot have been monozygotic, because identical twins are alike in every respect
Differences in the twins' environments over time altered their patterns of gene expression
The older twins who lived together must have differed genetically, since their environments were the same
optionWhy: A student who treats methylation as a mutation picks this. Methyl tags alter gene expression without altering the base sequence, so the twins remain genetically identical.

A student who takes 'identical' to cover gene activity as well as genome picks this. Monozygotic twins have the same DNA but can develop different epigenetic tags, which is exactly what makes them useful for this kind of study.

Monozygotic twins share a genome, so differences in methylation cannot be genetic. The growth of the differences with age, and especially with time apart, shows the environment acting on gene expression through epigenetic tags.
A student who equates environment with the home picks this. Twins living together still differ in diet, illness, habits and exposures, and monozygotic twins do not differ genetically.
questions.explain: Monozygotic twins share a genome, so differences in methylation cannot be genetic. The growth of the differences with age, and especially with time apart, shows the environment acting on gene expression through epigenetic tags.

questions.q: Sodium chloride dissolves when it is placed in water. Which statement describes the attractions that hold the ions in solution?
options: Na⁺ ions are attracted to the partially negative oxygen atoms of water molecules, and Cl⁻ ions to the partially positive hydrogen atoms.
Hydrogen bonds form between each ion and the water molecules that surround it, just as they form between water molecules.
Both kinds of ion are attracted to the oxygen end of the water molecules, because that is the end that carries a charge.
Water molecules react chemically with the sodium chloride, breaking it down into separate sodium and chlorine atoms.
optionWhy: Water is polar. Each positively charged Na⁺ ion is attracted to the partially negative oxygen atoms of surrounding water molecules, and each negatively charged Cl⁻ ion to the partially positive hydrogen atoms, so the ions are separated and held in solution.

A student who uses hydrogen bonding to explain every property of water picks this. Hydrogen bonds form between water and polar molecules such as glucose; an ion is held in solution by the attraction between its charge and the partial charges on water.

A student who has only seen a hydrated sodium ion drawn picks this. The hydrogen atoms of water carry partial positive charges, so it is the hydrogen end that is attracted to a negatively charged chloride ion.
A student who thinks of dissolving as a chemical change picks this. No reaction occurs: the ions stay as Na⁺ and Cl⁻ and are simply separated and surrounded by water molecules.
questions.explain: Water is polar. Each positively charged Na⁺ ion is attracted to the partially negative oxygen atoms of surrounding water molecules, and each negatively charged Cl⁻ ion to the partially positive hydrogen atoms, so the ions are separated and held in solution.

questions.q: Five potato cylinders were bathed in 0.4 mol dm⁻³ sucrose. Their percentage changes in mass had a mean of −3.0%, a standard deviation of 1.0% and a standard error of 0.45%. What does the standard error indicate?
options: The average size of the mistakes made in weighing the cylinders, which would be zero if the balance had been used correctly.
The spread of the five individual percentage changes around their mean, which is the same thing that the standard deviation shows.
How close the sample mean of −3.0% is likely to be to the true mean; it would decrease if more cylinders were measured.
The maximum and minimum percentage changes recorded, so every cylinder lost between 2.55% and 3.45% of its mass.
optionWhy: A student who reads 'error' as 'mistake' picks this. Standard error reflects natural variation between samples, not faults in technique; perfectly weighed cylinders that vary in their response still give a standard error above zero.

A student who treats the two statistics as one picks this. The spread of the individual values is described by the standard deviation of 1.0%; the standard error is a property of the mean, which is why it is smaller.

Standard error indicates the precision of the sample mean as an estimate of the true mean for this concentration. It is smaller than the standard deviation and falls as the number of repeats rises, and it can be shown graphically as error bars.
A student who reads error bars as a range picks this. Standard error is not the limits of the data: with a standard deviation of 1.0%, individual cylinders lie well outside 0.45% of the mean.
questions.explain: Standard error indicates the precision of the sample mean as an estimate of the true mean for this concentration. It is smaller than the standard deviation and falls as the number of repeats rises, and it can be shown graphically as error bars.

questions.q: A strip of onion epidermis is mounted in a concentrated sucrose solution and viewed under a microscope. Which statement describes what happens to its cells?
options: Water leaves each cell by osmosis and the whole cell, wall included, shrinks and crumples inward, just as an animal cell crenates.
Water leaves each cell by osmosis and an empty space forms between the wall and the membrane, because the wall lets nothing through.
Water leaves each cell by osmosis, the protoplast shrinks and its membrane pulls away from the wall: the cells are plasmolysed.
Water enters each cell by osmosis, because the concentrated solution is hypotonic to them, and the cells become turgid.
optionWhy: A student who transfers crenation to plant cells picks this. The rigid cellulose wall keeps its shape; only the protoplast inside it shrinks.
A student who treats the wall as a barrier picks this. The cell wall is freely permeable, so the space that opens up is filled by the sucrose solution.

The concentrated sucrose solution is hypertonic to the cell sap, so water leaves by osmosis. The protoplast shrinks and the membrane pulls away from the wall, which keeps its shape: this is plasmolysis.
A student who has swapped hypo- and hyper- picks this. A concentrated solution has the higher solute concentration, so it is hypertonic and water leaves the cells.
questions.explain: The concentrated sucrose solution is hypertonic to the cell sap, so water leaves by osmosis. The protoplast shrinks and the membrane pulls away from the wall, which keeps its shape: this is plasmolysis.

questions.q: A kidney removed for transplantation is bathed in a solution while it is stored. Which type of solution is used, and why?
options: Sterile distilled water, so that the cells stay well hydrated and no solutes can enter the organ before it is transplanted.
An isotonic solution, so that the kidney's cells neither gain nor lose water by net osmosis while the organ is stored.
A slightly hypotonic solution, so that the cells are kept fully hydrated by a steady inward flow of water.
A hypotonic solution, so that the cells take in water and become turgid, keeping the organ firm during storage.
optionWhy: A student who regards pure water as the safest fluid picks this. Distilled water is hypotonic to the cells, which would take in water by osmosis, swell and burst.

A solution with the same solute concentration as the cytoplasm of the kidney's cells prevents net osmotic movement of water in either direction, so the cells are not damaged by swelling or shrinkage before transplantation.
A student who thinks extra water is good for cells picks this. A hypotonic solution would cause a net inflow of water into cells that lack walls, and they would swell and burst.
A student who expects animal cells to become turgid picks this. Turgidity needs a cell wall; the cells of a kidney have none, so water entering them causes swelling and bursting, not firmness.
questions.explain: A solution with the same solute concentration as the cytoplasm of the kidney's cells prevents net osmotic movement of water in either direction, so the cells are not damaged by swelling or shrinkage before transplantation.

questions.q: Two adjacent plant cells have water potentials of −300 kPa (cell A) and −900 kPa (cell B). Which statement describes the net movement of water between them?
options: From B to A, because −900 kPa is the larger number, so the water in B has the greater potential energy.
There is no net movement, because both values are negative, so neither cell's water has any potential energy.
From A to B only if the cells use energy to pump it, because water cannot move down a gradient by itself.
From A to B, because water moves from higher to lower water potential and loses potential energy.
optionWhy: A student who compares magnitudes and ignores the sign picks this. −900 kPa is further below zero than −300 kPa, so B has the lower water potential and its water has less potential energy.
A student who treats the scale as absolute picks this. Negative values are relative to pure water; the water in both cells has potential energy, and there is more of it in A than in B.
A student who thinks water movement is active picks this. Water moves down a water potential gradient passively, without any input of energy from the cells.

−300 kPa is the higher water potential, so cell A's water has more potential energy per unit volume than cell B's. Water moves from higher to lower water potential, losing potential energy as it does so, until the two are equal.
questions.explain: −300 kPa is the higher water potential, so cell A's water has more potential energy per unit volume than cell B's. Water moves from higher to lower water potential, losing potential energy as it does so, until the two are equal.

questions.q: Plant tissue is bathed in a sucrose solution with a water potential of −2500 kPa. The cells initially have a solute potential of −900 kPa and a pressure potential of +600 kPa. Which statement explains what happens?
options: Water leaves the cells; pressure potential becomes negative as the shrinking protoplast pulls inward on the cell wall that surrounds it.
Water leaves the cells; the wall contracts with the protoplast, so the pressure potential stays positive as the cell shrinks.
Water leaves the cells; the sap becomes more concentrated, so ψs rises above zero and the water potential of every cell becomes positive.
Water leaves the cells; pressure potential falls to zero as the protoplast pulls away from the wall, so ψw equals ψs for each cell.
optionWhy: A student who applies xylem tension to any cell under strain picks this. Once the protoplast shrinks away from the wall there is no wall pressure on it, so the pressure potential is zero, not negative.
A student who thinks the whole cell shrinks like a crenating animal cell picks this. The rigid wall keeps its shape; the protoplast pulls away from it and the pressure potential falls to zero.

A student who expects concentrated solutions to have positive values picks this. Concentrating the sap makes its solute potential more negative, and the cell's water potential falls towards −2500 kPa.

The cells start at ψw = −900 + 600 = −300 kPa, far above the solution's −2500 kPa, so water leaves. As the protoplast shrinks the wall stops pressing on it, ψp falls to zero and the cells plasmolyse; from incipient plasmolysis onward ψw = ψs, which becomes more negative as the sap concentrates.
questions.explain: The cells start at ψw = −900 + 600 = −300 kPa, far above the solution's −2500 kPa, so water leaves. As the protoplast shrinks the wall stops pressing on it, ψp falls to zero and the cells plasmolyse; from incipient plasmolysis onward ψw = ψs, which becomes more negative as the sap concentrates.
